extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proofs / introductory set theory
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook chapter explaining basic set theory concepts (elements vs. subsets, power sets, unions/intersections/differences, complements, Venn diagrams, indexed sets) intended to prepare students for proof-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element versus subset distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between an object being an element of a set (x ∈ A) and being a subset of a set (X ⊆ A); an element need not be a set, and sets themselves can be elements of other sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in {1, {1}}, 1 is the first element and {1} is the second element; you cannot select 1 from {1,{1}} to make the subset {1} by selecting 1 (you must select {1} to make {{1}}). Watch for confusing expressions like {1} ∈ B vs {1} ⊆ B; anti-patterns illustrated by incorrect listings in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of subset (⊆)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set X is a subset of A (X ⊆ A) iff every element of X is also an element of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly in examples and exercises; reasoning about membership vs subset-hood is essential when forming subsets or power sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set definition (P(A))
rubrics_metrics.description: The power set P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. In symbols, P(A) = {X : X ⊆ A}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if A = {1,2,3} then P(A) = {∅, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {1,2,3}}. When A is finite with n elements, P(A) can be listed explicitly; when A is infinite, P(A) is typically not listable but contains all subsets (including graphs, images, and arbitrary subsets of R^2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set cardinality for finite sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is finite with n elements, then |P(A)| = 2^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact 1.4 and examples demonstrate counting the subsets to get 2^n. Exercises and examples show verifying |P(A)| = 2^n for small finite A and exploring cardinalities for combinations like P(A)×P(B) etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union, intersection, and difference definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For sets A and B: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}; A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}; A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation in words: union = in A or B (or both); intersection = in both; difference = elements in A but not in B. Examples: A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A−B computed for concrete finite sets and in Cartesian-product contexts. Note difference is not commutative (X−Y ≠ Y−X in general).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product and interaction with set operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cartesian product A × B is the set of ordered pairs (a,b) with a ∈ A and b ∈ B; set operations distribute in examples involving products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (A − B) × B listed; (A × C) ∩ (B × C) = (A ∩ B) × C illustrated by listing pairs. Use product notation when shading or constructing subsets in R^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interval notation and set operations on intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use interval notation [a,b], (a,b], etc., as shorthand for subsets of R and apply union/intersection/difference to intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [2,5] ∪ [3,6] = [2,6]; [2,5] ∩ [3,6] = [3,5]; [2,5] − [3,6] = [2,3). Exercises ask for sketching and reasoning on number line to determine results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal set and complement
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a set A with universal set U, the complement A^c (denoted A with bar or A) is U − A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the natural universal set for the context (e.g., primes P ⊆ N, unit circle C ⊆ R^2). Examples: P^c (composite numbers plus 1) when U = N; graphical shading of complements in R^2. Be explicit about U when taking complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venn diagram usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Venn diagrams are informal schematic diagrams that represent sets (usually as circles) and illustrate how sets combine under operations like union, intersection, and difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Venn diagrams as scratch-work devices to visualize and develop strategies for proofs or problems. Diagrams for two and three sets are shown with different shadings to represent unions, intersections, and differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses rules for set expressions (important point)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expression uses only ∪ (or only ∩), parentheses are optional (associativity); if it uses both ∪ and ∩, parentheses are essential because the expression is ambiguous without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A ∪ B ∪ C = (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C); but A ∪ B ∩ C is ambiguous—must specify (A ∪ B) ∩ C or A ∪ (B ∩ C). Venn diagrams illustrate that (A ∪ B) ∩ C and A ∪ (B ∩ C) yield different regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed sets and sigma-like notation for unions/intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: For a collection A_1, A_2, …, A_n (or infinite), use notation ∪_{i=1}^n A_i and ∩_{i=1}^n A_i to denote the union and intersection respectively; this generalizes to index sets I: ∪_{a ∈ I} A_a and ∩_{a ∈ I} A_a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The index set I need not be integers—it can be any set (e.g., real numbers). Define union as {x : x ∈ A_a for at least one a ∈ I} and intersection as {x : x ∈ A_a for every a ∈ I}. Examples include infinite unions producing geometric regions and intersections producing single points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed-sets examples illustrating nontrivial unions/intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete indexed examples show behavior of unions/intersections: e.g., rectangles A_a = [a,2] × [0,a] for a ∈ [0,2] have union equal to a triangle and intersection equal to a single point {(2,0)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through why a point belongs to all A_a or at least one A_a; these examples demonstrate subtleties when the index set is uncountable or continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union and intersection notation conventions and subset relations for collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation ∪_{a ∈ I} A_a and ∩_{a ∈ I} A_a extends to arbitrary collections; consider relations such as whether ∩_{a ∈ J} A_a ⊆ ∪_{a ∈ I} A_a under changes to index sets J and I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises probe questions like: If J ⊆ I then what subset relations hold between the unions/intersections over J and I? Use these to reason about containment and equality of indexed unions/intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs and images as subsets of R^2 (and elements of P(R^2))
rubrics_metrics.description: The graph of a function y = f(x) is the set G = {(x, f(x)) : x ∈ R}, hence a subset of R^2 and therefore an element of P(R^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any function's graph and any black-and-white image on the plane can be regarded as elements of P(R^2); this highlights the vastness of P(R^2) and why explicit listing is impossible for infinite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with listing and common power-set mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: When listing elements or subsets, ensure the distinction between elements and singleton sets is respected; many incorrect listings stem from treating an element and the singleton containing it as the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wrong examples are given (e.g., listing {{1}} as an element when it is not) with explanations stressing why listings are incorrect. Check membership carefully when forming P(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Any non-empty subset of N has a smallest element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is used often in proofs (sometimes without explicit naming) and underlies arguments like the division algorithm—students should be comfortable invoking it when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division algorithm (existence via well-ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given integers a and b with b > 0, there exist unique integers q and r with a = qb + r and 0 ≤ r < b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: form A = {a − xb : x ∈ Z, 0 ≤ a − xb}, apply well-ordering to get the least element r; uniqueness is an exercise. Understand this as an application of the well-ordering principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of numbers as sets (brief remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural numbers can be modeled as sets: 0 = ∅, 1 = {∅}, 2 = {∅,{∅}}, etc.; in this approach every mathematical entity can be defined in set-theoretic terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes this construction exists but does not develop it further; it's a conceptual point rather than a required technique for most exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell's paradox and foundational caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The naive comprehension 'A = {X : X ∉ X}' leads to Russell's paradox (is A ∈ A?), which motivated careful axiomatization of set theory (Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms) including the axiom of foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the paradox as a warning about careless set construction; accepting standard axioms avoids such paradoxes. The point is background motivation rather than everyday usage for elementary set operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mathematical statement (beginning of logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is a sentence or mathematical expression that is either definitely true or definitely false (used in logic to deduce information).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of true/false statements and non-statements are given; notation P(x) for statements with variables is introduced. This is preparatory for use of statements in proofs.
